questions.prompt: How are LLM API calls typically billed?

options.text: A flat fee per API call regardless of size
By tokens: everything sent in (prompt + context) and everything generated out, priced per million tokens
By the seconds of compute time used
By the number of correct answers

questions.explanation: Input and output tokens are metered separately, priced per million. Every word of system prompt, retrieved document, and chat history is on the bill — every single call.

questions.prompt: At $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, roughly what does a call with 10,000 input tokens and 1,000 output tokens cost?
questions.explanation: Input: 10,000 ÷ 1,000,000 × $3 = $0.03. Output: 1,000 ÷ 1,000,000 × $15 = $0.015. Total ≈ $0.045. Pennies per call — until you multiply by a million calls.

questions.prompt: Why do output tokens usually cost several times more than input tokens?

options.text: Generating tokens is sequential — one at a time, each requiring a full pass — while reading input can be processed in parallel
Providers charge more for whatever users want most

questions.explanation: Reading (prefill) parallelizes; generation is inherently one-token-at-a-time. That asymmetry in compute shows up directly in the price sheet — and is a reason to constrain response length.

questions.prompt: Which habits leak money in an AI product? (select all that apply)

options.text: A 3,000-token system prompt resent with every one of a million daily calls
Retrieving 20 document chunks when 3 would answer the question
Long chats that resend the entire conversation history each turn
Asking the model for a one-paragraph answer instead of an essay

questions.explanation: Repeated bloat, over-retrieval, and unbounded history are the classic leaks — each re-billed on every call. Constraining output length (d) SAVES money. Trimming context also tends to improve answer quality, as module 10 will show.
